newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia oil/metal stake sales spur controversy.
newsitem.headline: Russia oil/metal stake sales spur controversy.

text.p: Confusion and controversy surround the latest and nearly last leg of Russia's huge privatisation programme as stakes in a major oil company and a mining and metals giant go under the hammer.

A 40 percent stake in the Tyumen Oil Company (TNK) went exactly where it was expected on Friday -- to Alfa-Bank -- while potential bidders in this week's tender of 38 percent of metals mammoth Norilsk Nickel object to terms of the sale.
"Yes, I did expect Alfa to win the Tyumen stake and no, these tenders are not always fair," said Ivan Mazalov, oil and gas analyst at CentreInvest Group consultancy in Moscow.
His comments had a familiar ring. Foreigners are limited to 15 percent of firms deemed strategically important for Russia, including many prize assets in the natural resources sector.
Potential overseas bidders charge that the rule robs Russia of much-needed cash. Competition would be hotter with foreign companies taking part, forcing bids higher, they say.
London-based commodity powerhouse Trans-World Group, already a force in Russian aluminium, said it would bid in the Norilsk tender if it was allowed and if the terms were fairer.
In a letter sent to the government on Friday, Trans-World proposed postponing the Norilsk tender, due to open on Tuesday.

With results of the sale scheduled for August 5, Trans-World has left its attempt to put off the sale to the last minute. But analysts do not rule out completely the possibility of the tender being postponed or its terms changed.

"It's a question of the government's reaction to the letter -- it is difficult to say whether they will change the terms of the tender or not," said Tatyana Nikolskaya, analyst at Pioneer Securities in Moscow.
And on the eve of the opening of the tender, the question of foreigners' participation remains unresolved.

Uneximbank on Monday repeated its belief that the 15 percent foreign limit holds, barring overseas bids because the 38 percent stake -- a majority of the voting shares -- must be sold in a single lot. Russia's Federal Property Fund says there are no restrictions for foreigners.

Norilsk could become the world's biggest nickel producer this year. But Uneximbank has struggled to rescue the firm, still burdened by the huge social costs of supporting the Arctic city of Norilsk, where its flagship plant is based.
In the case of TNK, infighting among Russian bidders shows that personalities and politics still hold sway when it comes to choosing winners and loosers in post-Soviet privatisation.

A unit of Alfa-Bank, itself part of the powerful Alfa Group conglomerate, announced on Friday it had won a tender for 40 percent of TNK, Russia's sixth largest oil company by output with enormous but hard-to-recover reserves.

The announcement follows a bitter row between Alfa and the head of TNK's main production unit, Nizhnevartovskneftegaz. Viktor Pali has said Alfa Group units had stakes in equipment and assets, giving them the edge in the tender.
The spat triggered high-level promises of fair conditions in the sale. But analysts said the outcome was never in much doubt, partly because of close links between Alfa and the government.
"Alfa-Bank was obviously one of those companies which contributed to the presidential election campaign," said one.
Pyotr Aven, foreign trade minister in 1992, heads Alfa-Bank and is part of an elite group of bankers and businessmen said to have supported Boris Yeltsin's 1996 re-election.
Alfa offered $820 million for the stake and investments. It was the highest bid but still cheap considering TNK's reserves.
Mazalov said that based on the most conservative estimates of TNK oil reserves, the Alfa bid valued them at $4 per tonne -- about average for Russia but cheap in international terms.
Alexei Kokin, energy analyst at Renaissance Capital, said Alfa should bid for another 11 percent of TNK in a separate cash auction next month, giving it full control of the oil group.
